title: How Compiler Explorer Runs on AWS in 2026 — Matt Godbolt’s blog
excerpt: A tour of the AWS services behind every Compiler Explorer compilation
content_html:
Written with LLM assistance.
Details at end.

I’ve been meaning to write an update on how Compiler Explorer actually runs on Amazon’s cloud, and it’s been sat on my list for a good while now, somewhere behind the other random things that take up what laughably I refer to as my spare time1.

The last time I wrote about this was 2016, when the whole site was a load balancer, a couple of instances and some Docker containers I built on my laptop. I wrote a much longer how it works last summer, but that one is mostly about Compiler Explorer and only incidentally about the cloud it sits on.

It’s no secret that we run on AWS, and none of it is hidden: the infra repository has all the terraform, the install scripts and the ce command line tool we drive the whole thing with, so if you’d rather read the real thing than my description of it, help yourself. So this one goes the other way round, through the Amazon services we lean on, roughly in the order your compile request runs into them.

Getting your code as far as our servers

Your browser talks to CloudFront, Amazon’s CDN. We run two separate CloudFront distributions. The one in front of godbolt.org mostly just hands requests on to our load balancer, caching what it sensibly can and compressing things on the way back out2. The bulky static stuff lives in an S3 bucket behind a second distribution at static.ce-cdn.net: the compiled JavaScript, the images, the web fonts. Much the largest part of that is Monaco, the editor component out of Visual Studio Code, which is what gives you the syntax highlighting and the squiggly underlines and the rest of it. It’s a lot of JavaScript to send someone who only wants to look at some assembly, so it’s worth having it cached near them.

Sitting in front of that is WAF, doing our rate limiting. Our limits are very simple and very high, mostly because we used to be stricter and it kept catching C++ trainers: a whole classroom behind a conference’s NAT looks like a single very keen IP address. We could probably do something cleverer with fingerprinting, but raising the limit was easier and it hasn’t been a problem since.3

Rather a lot of fleets behind one load balancer

Behind CloudFront is a single Application Load Balancer. It works out from the path which cluster a request is for, and then picks a healthy instance in that cluster to send it to. Almost everything has no special prefix at all and goes to the production fleet, which is where the overwhelming bulk of the traffic ends up. /beta* and /staging* go to the beta and staging fleets4. /winprod* goes to a fleet of Windows instances running MSVC, /aarch64prod* to Graviton machines that run ARM code natively rather than under emulation, and /gpu* to machines with real NVIDIA cards in them5.

Each of those is an Auto Scaling Group, and these days each one is doubled up: a blue and a green. To deploy, we bring up the other colour, wait for it to go healthy, point the load balancer’s target group at it and drain the old one. If it’s wrong, we point it back. Before that, deploying meant a rolling restart of the fleet with our ce command line tool, one instance at a time. That worked well enough, but backing out a bad release meant rolling the whole fleet forward again onto the previous version, which is a bit slow when you’ve just broken the site.

The scaling itself is simple: we just try and keep the average CPU load below a threshold. We’ve kicked around more sophisticated ideas but this one is supported out of the box6.

Renting the bits nobody else wants

The production fleet is almost entirely spot instances – unused EC2 capacity, sold off cheap, on the understanding that you can be evicted at two minutes’ notice. It’s a 60-90% saving over on-demand – quite a lot of money, for us.

We can get away with that because our instances don’t really matter. Everything that needs to survive lives on the shared filesystem, in S3 or in DynamoDB, so an instance that vanishes is just an instance that gets replaced. We ask for sixteen different instance types across the m5, m6, m7, r6 and i3/i4i families. The allocation strategy is price-capacity-optimized – Amazon’s way of saying “pick whichever of these is cheapest and least likely to get yanked”. In practice we get evicted, the scaling group notices, and a new one turns up.

Why the compilers are the hard part

We have around 6,000 compiler entries9 across 93 languages, and we never delete any of them7. Once a compiler version goes up it stays up, so that Stack Overflow answer showing a GCC 4.8 codegen quirk still compiles today. It’s our bit against link rot, and it does mean we hoard an awful lot of binaries.

All of that lives on EFS, Amazon’s elastic NFS, and NFS has latency. C-like languages pull in an enormous number of very small header files, so the naive version of this is unusably slow. Our fix, which sounds daft, is to build a SquashFS image per compiler, store the image also on EFS, and mount it through a loopback device. The kernel then thinks it’s talking to a local block device and caches blocks properly instead of checking with a server in another building every time10.

That worked, but it meant mounting a couple of thousand images at every boot, which took the best part of a minute and kept the metadata for thousands of filesystems resident in kernel memory. That cached metadata is a good chunk of why squashfs beats NFS in the first place, so it’s not wasted as such; it’s just that any one instance is only ever going to touch a handful of those compilers, so we were paying for all of it to use a fraction of it. It took me three years and several abandoned attempts to fix that, and the answer was CEFS: content-addressed images, packed into bundles of around 20GB, mounted on demand by autofs the first time something touches the path. The migration took us from 2,182 images down to 121, and OS startup from 50 seconds to 20! It’s crept back up to around 883 since, because the nightly builds keep making new images and consolidation only packs down whatever is already there. A garbage collection while I was writing this turned up 111 images that nothing references any more, about 63GiB’s worth8.

Our storage has come down a lot over the year too, though I’m honestly not sure how much of that is CEFS and how much is me finally deleting the old squash images:

Aug/04 01:55 admin-node~ $ df -h
Filesystem                                 Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
/dev/nvme0n1p1                              97G   20G   77G  21% /
fs-db4c8192.efs.us-east-1.amazonaws.com:/  8.0E  2.2T  8.0E   1% /opt

2.2T, where a year ago it was 3.9T. Still nowhere near 8 exabytes, mind.

Building compilers all night, every night

We build a pile of compilers from scratch every night: GCC trunk, Clang trunk, and a long tail of experimental branches for reflection, contracts, coroutines and all the other fun stuff. That’s 94 nightly build jobs at the moment11, up from 73 a year ago and 33 in 2022.

Those run on our own GitHub Actions runners on EC2, spun up on demand with the excellent terraform-aws-github-runner, with all the compiler orchestration on top being ours. Building trunk LLVM wants a big machine and a decent chunk of time, and GitHub’s hosted runners weren’t up to it when we set this up.

This is the part of the bill that goes up every time somebody asks us for another compiler and we say yes12.

The bits that are half-finished

One thing we’ve built but not finished rolling out is what we call the CE Router: a small fleet whose job is to decide where a compilation should happen, look the answer up in DynamoDB and drop the request on an SQS queue, with the result coming back to your browser over an API Gateway WebSocket. The point is to stop the machine that answers the HTTP request having to be the machine that owns the compiler.

It works, but it isn’t carrying production traffic yet: the load balancer rules that would send compilations through it are still commented out, and we’re migrating gradually. Your compile today still goes straight to a machine in the prod fleet, the way it always has.

Building it did turn up a good AWS gotcha, though. API Gateway WebSocket frames top out at 32KiB, and the assembly for almost any non-trivial program is bigger than that; in the other direction SQS messages cap out at 256KB, which a decent-sized multi-file project will go past. So in both directions, if the thing is too big we shove it in S3 and send a key instead.

Everything else

A scattering of other services doing one job each:

  • DynamoDB holds the short links. Every godbolt.org/z/... you’ve put in a slide deck is a row in a table, and there are a couple of million of them.
  • S3 holds the compilers we build, the static assets, the logs, and a daily-expiring content-addressable compilation cache, so the second person to compile the same thing gets it for free.
  • Lambda does the odd jobs: the Claude Explain backend, the nightly version tracking, and the one that pushes CloudWatch alarms into our Discord so it’s not just my phone buzzing at 3am.
  • Route 53, ACM, CloudTrail, Backup and SES are the plumbing. I don’t think about them much.
  • CloudWatch drives the auto-scaling triggers, though for actually looking at things we run Grafana, Prometheus and Loki. Those dashboards are public.

Everything is in us-east-1. If you’re compiling from Sydney your code goes a long way round, and I’m afraid it’s going to keep doing that: keeping a couple of terabytes of compilers in sync across regions would be an absolute nightmare.

Some numbers

We log a heavily anonymised JSON record to S3 for every compilation, with a Glue table over the top, so while writing this I went and counted them properly: 5,238,210 compilations in July, and 78.7 million over the last twelve months. It’s been sliding gently all year, down about a third from last autumn’s peak.


Compilations per month over the last year. Generated from this script.

The big drop before that, from 2024’s 14 million a month, I can at least half explain: in mid-2024 we doubled the default delay before we auto-recompile as you type, from 750ms to 1500ms, and then to 2 seconds13. If you type continuously, doubling that delay roughly halves the number of compilations you generate, without anybody noticing anything much. This latest slide isn’t that, though: it started well over a year later.

So I don’t really have a good explanation, and I can’t easily go and find one, because we deliberately don’t track who you are: no cookies, nothing that would let me tell you how many people used the site yesterday. I’d make that trade again every time, but it does leave me squinting at graphs occasionally.

Since I had the query open, here’s what folks actually compiled in July:

id                      compiles   compiler
g161                   1,386,532   GCC 16.1 (C++)
cg161                    403,659   GCC 16.1 (C)
gsnapshot                298,256   GCC trunk
clang_trunk              287,885   Clang trunk
g152                     239,331   GCC 15.2
clang2210                177,958   Clang 22.1
vcpp_v19_latest_x64      132,186   MSVC
r1970                     65,380   Rust 1.97
python314                 51,104   Python 3.14

That top entry is 26% of everything – roughly what you’d expect when you’re the default15. The load balancer sees around 14 million requests a month; our busiest day this year was the 21st of April at 1.44 million. The auto-scaling dealt with that one by itself; I only found out about it while writing this.

All of that costs us somewhere around $3,600 a month on AWS at the moment, which works out at about $0.0007 per compilation14. For the best part of a year we barely paid any of that: AWS’s open source credits covered almost all of it. Those ran out in the spring, we paid our own way for a few months, and AWS have just renewed them for another year, which is a huge help. Either way we’re fine for money, thanks to our Patreon supporters, our GitHub sponsors and our commercial sponsors. I did a full breakdown of the costs last year and it’s still roughly the right shape.


The wall of compilers, a year on: 6,157 entries across 93 languages.
Regenerated from the same script as last year's.

Things I’d still like to fix

Deployment is better than it was but there’s still more hand-holding in it than I’d like16. The CE Router migration has been “nearly done” for a while now… I still wish I’d laid out the NFS directory structure properly at the start instead of growing it one compiler at a time for a decade. And we moved everything to Ubuntu 24.04 this year, which was not the tidy little upgrade it sounds like17.

None of this is especially clever: it’s a load balancer, some scaling groups full of cheap spot instances, a network filesystem and a decade of accumulated hacks. It does keep working, though, and these days it mostly keeps working without anyone having to go and poke it. I’m pretty happy with that.

Thanks

As ever, the people who keep this running are the contributors. Partouf (Patrick Quist) above all – I really don’t know what CE would do without them – along with the core team and the many, many people who send PRs and file issues. Thank you all. Thanks too to AWS, whose open source credits programme paid for the best part of a year of everything described above, and who have just renewed for another year – which is not a small thing for a project our size, and it lets us get on with the interesting problems instead of watching the bill. Thank you AWS! And thanks, as always, to our Patreon and GitHub Sponsors supporters and our commercial sponsors, who cover the rest.

Questions? Complaints? Compilers we’re missing? Drop by our Discord, or find me on Bluesky or Mastodon.

Disclaimer

This article was a collaboration between a human and an LLM. I set it off to dig through our infrastructure repositories and our AWS account for the current numbers, which turned up several things I had wrong, and worked from that. It also ran the Athena queries and regenerated the graphs. The opinions, em- and en-dashes, and mistakes are all mine.

  1. In my defence, those have included a month back in the UK dealing with some family things, a run of C++ talks (C++Now, ACCU on Sea, CppCon, a keynote at C++ Under the Sea, and Meeting C++ in Berlin, where I’ll be going into a lot of this in rather more detail), some more Computerphile videos, and getting completely obsessed with how PAL decoding works. ↩

  2. We only got round to turning brotli compression on at the edge for the main app in June this year. ↩

  3. WAF also gives us a banned-ipv4 and a banned-ipv6 list that I add to by hand when we spot somebody misbehaving, and take them off again once they’ve got the hint. It doesn’t happen often: last year it was one anomalous IPv6 address, and an analytics outfit that was hammering us, who came off the list again the next day. Every now and again some enterprising soul works out that a site which compiles and runs arbitrary code is, if you squint, a free compute farm, but that’s rare and it tends to be pretty obvious. ↩

  4. Beta is very rarely used, but when we do have a longer-term experiment on the go that’s where it lives. Staging is for short-lived pre-deploy checks. ↩

  5. These cost a small fortune to run, but being able to see the results of running GPU code makes it worthwhile. We worked with our friends at NVIDIA to get the drivers and toolchains working properly, and they were a corporate sponsor for a good while too. Thank you NVIDIA! ↩

  6. The obvious better signal is queue depth: how many compilations are actually waiting, rather than how busy the CPUs happen to look. We already have scaling policies written against ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible for some of the environments, and once the queue-based compilation path is carrying real traffic everywhere that’s what we’d like to scale everything on. ↩

  7. Nearly never, anyway. Very occasionally an experimental build gets replaced, and the nightly builds replace themselves by definition: today’s GCC trunk quietly does away with yesterday’s. It’s the released versions that stay put forever. ↩

  8. Content addressing does at least make that safe to work out: an image that nothing links to is definitely unused, so the collection can be automatic rather than me squinting at filenames and hoping. A good chunk of those 111 will be yesterday’s nightly builds, quietly superseded by today’s. ↩

  9. 6,157 if you ask the API, but that’s cheating slightly: it counts the same GCC once for C, once for C++, once for Fortran and so on. Unique names, it’s 4,291. Last June the equivalent numbers were 4,724 and 81 languages, so we’re still growing pretty nicely, and almost none of that is me: folks keep turning up with a language I’d never heard of and a working PR. ↩

  10. Normally NFS caches data locally, but it still validates that cached metadata is fresh with the server via attribute caching. Even when the file data is cached you pay the network latency to check it hasn’t changed. Going via a loopback-mounted SquashFS image “launders” away the NFS-ness: the squashfs driver sees a local block device, and the kernel is blissfully unaware that behind those cached blocks is a file on NFS that could in theory change. For immutable compiler images this is a huge boon. ↩

  11. A “job” isn’t a compiler: some build one thing, some build a whole family. The builds kick off at midnight UTC and queue on our build infrastructure, and a separate workflow installs at 5:30am, and the two still have no idea about each other, so sometimes we install yesterday’s builds. It’s on the list. ↩

  12. We’re not completely daft about it: before a nightly build runs it checks whether any of the upstream repositories have had a commit in the last week, and if nothing’s moved it skips the build entirely. A quiet week on some experimental branch costs us nothing much. ↩

  13. #6669, if you want the gory details. It went out at 1500ms, then someone tried 2 seconds, then it got reverted, then it went back to 2 seconds ten days later. The current default is 2000ms. ↩

  14. Up from $0.00039 a year ago, and not because anything got dearer. The volume went down and the fixed costs – all that storage, and building all those compilers every night – stayed exactly where they were. ↩

  15. I did this same exercise back in 2014, out of nearly 2 million compiles in total, to work out whether I could retire GCC 4.4. The default then was clang++ 3.0.6 at 37%, so the shape of the list hasn’t changed much even if everything else has. I didn’t retire GCC 4.4, and it’s still there. ↩

  16. Mainly it’s our “compiler discovery” step: before a version goes out we go and ask every compiler on the machine what it actually is and what it calls itself, and write the answers to a JSON file the site then reads. It’s still a manual step and it can occasionally fall over, though I think I’ve made it rather more stable in a recent commit. I’m also experimenting with using LLM “scripts” to help where I can’t automate things directly in code: there are a lot of weird edge cases to handle and encoding all of them properly is tricky. ↩

  17. Modern glibc uses SHT_RELR relocations, which need binutils 2.38 or newer to link against, and 29 of our older GCCs ship their own ld that predates that. We tried rebuilding them all from source, which cascaded into a wall of libsanitizer incompatibilities, so we gave up and settled for symlinking those compilers’ ld to a newer one at install time instead. Partouf later rebuilt a couple of them properly. ↩

None of this is especially clever: it’s a load balancer, some scaling groups full of cheap spot instances, a network filesystem and a decade of accumulated hacks. It does keep working, though, and these days it mostly keeps working without anyone having to go and poke it. I’m pretty happy with that. Thanks As ever, the people who keep this running are the contributors. Partouf (Patrick Quist) above all – I really don’t know what CE would do without them – along with the core team and the many, many people who send PRs and file issues. Thank you all. Thanks too to AWS, whose open source credits programme paid for the best part of a year of everything described above, and who have just renewed for another year – which is not a small thing for a project our size, and it lets us get on with the interesting problems instead of watching the bill. Thank you AWS! And thanks, as always, to our Patreon and GitHub Sponsors supporters and our commercial sponsors, who cover the rest. Questions? Complaints? Compilers we’re missing? Drop by our Discord, or find me on Bluesky or Mastodon. Disclaimer This article was a collaboration between a human and an LLM. I set it off to dig through our infrastructure repositories and our AWS account for the current numbers, which turned up several things I had wrong, and worked from that. It also ran the Athena queries and regenerated the graphs. The opinions, em- and en-dashes, and mistakes are all mine. In my defence, those have included a month back in the UK dealing with some family things, a run of C++ talks (C++Now, ACCU on Sea, CppCon, a keynote at C++ Under the Sea, and Meeting C++ in Berlin, where I’ll be going into a lot of this in rather more detail), some more Computerphile videos, and getting completely obsessed with how PAL decoding works. ↩ We only got round to turning brotli compression on at the edge for the main app in June this year. ↩ WAF also gives us a banned-ipv4 and a banned-ipv6 list that I add to by hand when we spot somebody misbehaving, and take them off again once they’ve got the hint. It doesn’t happen often: last year it was one anomalous IPv6 address, and an analytics outfit that was hammering us, who came off the list again the next day. Every now and again some enterprising soul works out that a site which compiles and runs arbitrary code is, if you squint, a free compute farm, but that’s rare and it tends to be pretty obvious. ↩ Beta is very rarely used, but when we do have a longer-term experiment on the go that’s where it lives. Staging is for short-lived pre-deploy checks. ↩ These cost a small fortune to run, but being able to see the results of running GPU code makes it worthwhile. We worked with our friends at NVIDIA to get the drivers and toolchains working properly, and they were a corporate sponsor for a good while too. Thank you NVIDIA! ↩ The obvious better signal is queue depth: how many compilations are actually waiting, rather than how busy the CPUs happen to look. We already have scaling policies written against ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible for some of the environments, and once the queue-based compilation path is carrying real traffic everywhere that’s what we’d like to scale everything on. ↩ Nearly never, anyway. Very occasionally an experimental build gets replaced, and the nightly builds replace themselves by definition: today’s GCC trunk quietly does away with yesterday’s. It’s the released versions that stay put forever. ↩ Content addressing does at least make that safe to work out: an image that nothing links to is definitely unused, so the collection can be automatic rather than me squinting at filenames and hoping. A good chunk of those 111 will be yesterday’s nightly builds, quietly superseded by today’s. ↩ 6,157 if you ask the API, but that’s cheating slightly: it counts the same GCC once for C, once for C++, once for Fortran and so on. Unique names, it’s 4,291. Last June the equivalent numbers were 4,724 and 81 languages, so we’re still growing pretty nicely, and almost none of that is me: folks keep turning up with a language I’d never heard of and a working PR. ↩ Normally NFS caches data locally, but it still validates that cached metadata is fresh with the server via attribute caching. Even when the file data is cached you pay the network latency to check it hasn’t changed. Going via a loopback-mounted SquashFS image “launders” away the NFS-ness: the squashfs driver sees a local block device, and the kernel is blissfully unaware that behind those cached blocks is a file on NFS that could in theory change. For immutable compiler images this is a huge boon. ↩ A “job” isn’t a compiler: some build one thing, some build a whole family. The builds kick off at midnight UTC and queue on our build infrastructure, and a separate workflow installs at 5:30am, and the two still have no idea about each other, so sometimes we install yesterday’s builds. It’s on the list. ↩ We’re not completely daft about it: before a nightly build runs it checks whether any of the upstream repositories have had a commit in the last week, and if nothing’s moved it skips the build entirely. A quiet week on some experimental branch costs us nothing much. ↩ #6669, if you want the gory details. It went out at 1500ms, then someone tried 2 seconds, then it got reverted, then it went back to 2 seconds ten days later. The current default is 2000ms. ↩ Up from $0.00039 a year ago, and not because anything got dearer. The volume went down and the fixed costs – all that storage, and building all those compilers every night – stayed exactly where they were. ↩ I did this same exercise back in 2014, out of nearly 2 million compiles in total, to work out whether I could retire GCC 4.4. The default then was clang++ 3.0.6 at 37%, so the shape of the list hasn’t changed much even if everything else has. I didn’t retire GCC 4.4, and it’s still there. ↩ Mainly it’s our “compiler discovery” step: before a version goes out we go and ask every compiler on the machine what it actually is and what it calls itself, and write the answers to a JSON file the site then reads. It’s still a manual step and it can occasionally fall over, though I think I’ve made it rather more stable in a recent commit. I’m also experimenting with using LLM “scripts” to help where I can’t automate things directly in code: there are a lot of weird edge cases to handle and encoding all of them properly is tricky. ↩ Modern glibc uses SHT_RELR relocations, which need binutils 2.38 or newer to link against, and 29 of our older GCCs ship their own ld that predates that. We tried rebuilding them all from source, which cascaded into a wall of libsanitizer incompatibilities, so we gave up and settled for symlinking those compilers’ ld to a newer one at install time instead. Partouf later rebuilt a couple of them properly. ↩ Posted at 10:19:00 CDT on 5th August 2026.

blocks.html_en: Your browser talks to CloudFront, Amazon’s CDN. We run two separate CloudFront distributions. The one in front of godbolt.org mostly just hands requests on to our load balancer, caching what it sensibly can and compressing things on the way back out2. The bulky static stuff lives in an S3 bucket behind a second distribution at static.ce-cdn.net: the compiled JavaScript, the images, the web fonts. Much the largest part of that is Monaco, the editor component out of Visual Studio Code, which is what gives you the syntax highlighting and the squiggly underlines and the rest of it. It’s a lot of JavaScript to send someone who only wants to look at some assembly, so it’s worth having it cached near them.

blocks.html_en: Behind CloudFront is a single Application Load Balancer. It works out from the path which cluster a request is for, and then picks a healthy instance in that cluster to send it to. Almost everything has no special prefix at all and goes to the production fleet, which is where the overwhelming bulk of the traffic ends up. /beta* and /staging* go to the beta and staging fleets4. /winprod* goes to a fleet of Windows instances running MSVC, /aarch64prod* to Graviton machines that run ARM code natively rather than under emulation, and /gpu* to machines with real NVIDIA cards in them5.

blocks.html_en: Each of those is an Auto Scaling Group, and these days each one is doubled up: a blue and a green. Before that, deploying meant a rolling restart of the fleet with our ce command line tool, one instance at a time. That worked well enough, but backing out a bad release meant rolling the whole fleet forward again onto the previous version, which is a bit slow when you’ve just broken the site.

blocks.html_en: We can get away with that because our instances don’t really matter. Everything that needs to survive lives on the shared filesystem, in S3 or in DynamoDB, so an instance that vanishes is just an instance that gets replaced. We ask for sixteen different instance types across the m5, m6, m7, r6 and i3/i4i families. The allocation strategy is price-capacity-optimized – Amazon’s way of saying “pick whichever of these is cheapest and least likely to get yanked”. In practice we get evicted, the scaling group notices, and a new one turns up.

sentences.zh: 我们可以侥幸逃脱，因为我们的实例并不重要。

sentences.zh: 我们要求提供 m5、m6、m7、r6 和 i3/i4i 系列中的 16 种不同实例类型。

sentences.en: Why the compilers are the hard part
sentences.zh: 为什么编译器是最难的部分

blocks.html_en: We have around 6,000 compiler entries9 across 93 languages, and we never delete any of them7. Once a compiler version goes up it stays up, so that Stack Overflow answer showing a GCC 4.8 codegen quirk still compiles today. It’s our bit against link rot, and it does mean we hoard an awful lot of binaries.

sentences.en: We have around 6,000 compiler entries9 across 93 languages, and we never delete any of them7.
sentences.zh: 我们有 93 种语言的大约 6,000 个编译器条目 9，并且我们从不删除其中任何一个 7。

sentences.en: Once a compiler version goes up it stays up, so that Stack Overflow answer showing a GCC 4.8 codegen quirk still compiles today.
sentences.zh: 一旦编译器版本上升，它就会保持不变，因此显示 GCC 4.8 codegen 怪癖的 Stack Overflow 答案今天仍然可以编译。

sentences.en: It’s our bit against link rot, and it does mean we hoard an awful lot of binaries.
sentences.zh: 这是我们反对链接腐烂的一点，这确实意味着我们囤积了大量的二进制文件。

blocks.html_en: All of that lives on EFS, Amazon’s elastic NFS, and NFS has latency. C-like languages pull in an enormous number of very small header files, so the naive version of this is unusably slow. Our fix, which sounds daft, is to build a SquashFS image per compiler, store the image also on EFS, and mount it through a loopback device. The kernel then thinks it’s talking to a local block device and caches blocks properly instead of checking with a server in another building every time10.

sentences.en: All of that lives on EFS, Amazon’s elastic NFS, and NFS has latency.
sentences.zh: 所有这些都依赖于 EFS（Amazon 的弹性 NFS），并且 NFS 存在延迟。

sentences.en: C-like languages pull in an enormous number of very small header files, so the naive version of this is unusably slow.
sentences.zh: 类 C 语言会引入大量非常小的头文件，因此其简单版本速度慢得无法使用。

sentences.en: Our fix, which sounds daft, is to build a SquashFS image per compiler, store the image also on EFS, and mount it through a loopback device.
sentences.zh: 我们的修复方案（听起来很愚蠢）是为每个编译器构建一个 SquashFS 映像，将该映像也存储在 EFS 上，并通过环回设备挂载它。

sentences.en: The kernel then thinks it’s talking to a local block device and caches blocks properly instead of checking with a server in another building every time10.
sentences.zh: 然后，内核认为它正在与本地块设备通信并正确缓存块，而不是每次都与另一个建筑物中的服务器进行检查10。

blocks.html_en: That worked, but it meant mounting a couple of thousand images at every boot, which took the best part of a minute and kept the metadata for thousands of filesystems resident in kernel memory. That cached metadata is a good chunk of why squashfs beats NFS in the first place, so it’s not wasted as such; it’s just that any one instance is only ever going to touch a handful of those compilers, so we were paying for all of it to use a fraction of it. It took me three years and several abandoned attempts to fix that, and the answer was CEFS: content-addressed images, packed into bundles of around 20GB, mounted on demand by autofs the first time something touches the path. The migration took us from 2,182 images down to 121, and OS startup from 50 seconds to 20! It’s crept back up to around 883 since, because the nightly builds keep making new images and consolidation only packs down whatever is already there. A garbage collection while I was writing this turned up 111 images that nothing references any more, about 63GiB’s worth8.

sentences.en: That worked, but it meant mounting a couple of thousand images at every boot, which took the best part of a minute and kept the metadata for thousands of filesystems resident in kernel memory.
sentences.zh: 这确实有效，但这意味着每次启动时都要安装几千个映像，这需要一分钟的时间，并将数千个文件系统的元数据保存在内核内存中。

sentences.en: That cached metadata is a good chunk of why squashfs beats NFS in the first place, so it’s not wasted as such; it’s just that any one instance is only ever going to touch a handful of those compilers, so we were paying for all of it to use a fraction of it.
sentences.zh: 缓存的元数据是squashfs 击败 NFS 的重要原因，因此它不会被浪费；只是任何一个实例只会接触其中的少数编译器，因此我们为所有实例付费以使用其中的一小部分。

sentences.en: It took me three years and several abandoned attempts to fix that, and the answer was CEFS: content-addressed images, packed into bundles of around 20GB, mounted on demand by autofs the first time something touches the path.
sentences.zh: 我花了三年时间并多次放弃尝试来解决这个问题，答案是 CEFS：内容寻址图像，打包成大约 20GB 的捆绑包，在第一次接触路径时由 autofs 按需安装。

sentences.en: The migration took us from 2,182 images down to 121, and OS startup from 50 seconds to 20!
sentences.zh: 此次迁移使我们将图像从 2,182 个减少到 121 个，操作系统启动时间从 50 秒减少到 20 秒！

sentences.en: It’s crept back up to around 883 since, because the nightly builds keep making new images and consolidation only packs down whatever is already there.
sentences.zh: 从那以后，它又回升至 883 左右，因为每晚构建都会不断生成新图像，而整合只会打包已有的图像。

sentences.en: A garbage collection while I was writing this turned up 111 images that nothing references any more, about 63GiB’s worth8.
sentences.zh: 当我写这篇文章时，垃圾收集发现了 111 个不再有任何引用的图像，大约 63GiB 的价值8。

blocks.html_en: Our storage has come down a lot over the year too, though I’m honestly not sure how much of that is CEFS and how much is me finally deleting the old squash images:

blocks.html_en: • Normally NFS caches data locally, but it still validates that cached metadata is fresh with the server via attribute caching. Even when the file data is cached you pay the network latency to check it hasn’t changed. Going via a loopback-mounted SquashFS image “launders” away the NFS-ness: the squashfs driver sees a local block device, and the kernel is blissfully unaware that behind those cached blocks is a file on NFS that could in theory change. For immutable compiler images this is a huge boon. ↩

content_html_zh:
在法学硕士的帮助下撰写。详细信息在最后。

我一直想写一篇关于 Compiler Explorer 如何在 Amazon 云上实际运行的更新，它已经在我的列表中呆了很长一段时间了，排在其他随机的事情后面，这些事情占用了我可笑的业余时间 1。

我上次写这篇文章是在 2016 年，当时整个站点都是一个负载均衡器、几个实例和我在笔记本电脑上构建的一些 Docker 容器。 去年夏天我写了一篇更长的文章，介绍它的工作原理，但那篇文章主要是关于编译器资源管理器的，只是顺便提到了它所在的云。

我们在 AWS 上运行已经不是什么秘密了，所有这些都不是隐藏的：基础设施存储库包含我们驱动整个系统的所有 terraform、安装脚本和 ce 命令行工具，因此，如果您更愿意阅读真实的内容而不是我的描述，请自行了解。 因此，这个过程正好相反，通过我们依赖的 Amazon 服务，大致按照您的编译请求运行到它们的顺序。

将您的代码传输至我们的服务器

您的浏览器与 Amazon 的 CDN CloudFront 进行通信。 我们运行两个独立的 CloudFront 发行版。 godbolt.org 前面的大部分只是将请求传递给我们的负载均衡器，缓存它合理可以存储的内容，并在返回时压缩内容2。 庞大的静态内容位于 static.ce-cdn.net 的第二个发行版后面的 S3 存储桶中：已编译的 JavaScript、图像、Web 字体。 其中最大的部分是 Monaco，它是 Visual Studio Code 中的编辑器组件，它为您提供语法突出显示和波浪下划线以及其他功能。 向只想查看某个程序集的人发送大量 JavaScript 代码，因此值得将其缓存在他们附近。

坐在前面的是 WAF，负责进行速率限制。 我们的限制非常简单，也非常高，主要是因为我们过去更加严格，这一直困扰着 C++ 培训师：会议 NAT 后面的整个教室看起来就像一个非常敏感的 IP 地址。 我们或许可以通过指纹识别做一些更聪明的事情，但提高限制更容易，而且从那以后就不再是问题了。3

一个负载均衡器后面有很多车队

CloudFront 背后是一个应用程序负载均衡器。 它根据请求所在集群的路径计算出，然后选择该集群中的一个健康实例将其发送到。 几乎所有东西都没有特殊的前缀，并进入生产队列，这是绝大多数流量的最终目的地。 /beta* 和 /staging* 进入 beta 和 staging 舰队4。 /winprod* 指向一组运行 MSVC 的 Windows 实例，/aarch64prod* 指向本地运行 ARM 代码而不是模拟的 Graviton 机器，/gpu* 指向带有真正 NVIDIA 卡的机器5。

其中每一个都是一个 Auto Scaling 组，现在每个组都是双倍的：蓝色和绿色。 为了部署，我们调出另一种颜色，等待它正常运行，将负载均衡器的目标组指向它并耗尽旧的颜色。 如果错了，我们会指出来。 在此之前，部署意味着使用我们的 ce 命令行工具滚动重新启动队列，一次一个实例。 这工作得很好，但是退出一个糟糕的版本意味着将整个舰队再次滚动到以前的版本，当你刚刚破坏了网站时，这有点慢。

扩展本身很简单：我们只是尝试将平均 CPU 负载保持在阈值以下。 我们已经提出了更复杂的想法，但这个想法是开箱即用的6。

租用别人不想要的部分

生产队列几乎完全是现货实例 - 未使用的 EC2 容量，低价出售，前提是您可以在提前两分钟通知时被驱逐。 与按需服务相比，这可以节省 60-90%，这对我们来说是一笔相当大的钱。

我们可以侥幸逃脱，因为我们的实例并不重要。 生存所需的一切都存在于共享文件系统、S3 或 DynamoDB 中，因此消失的实例只是被替换的实例。 我们要求提供 m5、m6、m7、r6 和 i3/i4i 系列中的 16 种不同实例类型。 分配策略是价格容量优化的——亚马逊的说法是“选择其中最便宜且最不可能被淘汰的”。 在实践中，我们被驱逐了，扩展组注意到了，然后一个新的出现了。

为什么编译器是最难的部分

我们有 93 种语言的大约 6,000 个编译器条目 9，并且我们从不删除其中任何一个 7。 一旦编译器版本上升，它就会保持不变，因此显示 GCC 4.8 codegen 怪癖的 Stack Overflow 答案今天仍然可以编译。 这是我们反对链接腐烂的一点，这确实意味着我们囤积了大量的二进制文件。

所有这些都依赖于 EFS（Amazon 的弹性 NFS），并且 NFS 存在延迟。 类 C 语言会引入大量非常小的头文件，因此其简单版本速度慢得无法使用。 我们的修复方案（听起来很愚蠢）是为每个编译器构建一个 SquashFS 映像，将该映像也存储在 EFS 上，并通过环回设备挂载它。 然后，内核认为它正在与本地块设备通信并正确缓存块，而不是每次都与另一个建筑物中的服务器进行检查10。

这确实有效，但这意味着每次启动时都要安装几千个映像，这需要一分钟的时间，并将数千个文件系统的元数据保存在内核内存中。 缓存的元数据是squashfs 击败 NFS 的重要原因，因此它不会被浪费；只是任何一个实例只会接触其中的少数编译器，因此我们为所有实例付费以使用其中的一小部分。 我花了三年时间并多次放弃尝试来解决这个问题，答案是 CEFS：内容寻址图像，打包成大约 20GB 的捆绑包，在第一次接触路径时由 autofs 按需安装。 此次迁移使我们将图像从 2,182 个减少到 121 个，操作系统启动时间从 50 秒减少到 20 秒！ 从那以后，它又回升至 883 左右，因为每晚构建都会不断生成新图像，而整合只会打包已有的图像。 当我写这篇文章时，垃圾收集发现了 111 个不再有任何引用的图像，大约 63GiB 的价值8。

我们的存储空间在这一年里也下降了很多，不过老实说我不确定其中有多少是 CEFS 以及我最终删除了旧的南瓜图像有多少：

Aug/04 01:55 admin-node~ $ df -h
Filesystem                                 Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
/dev/nvme0n1p1                              97G   20G   77G  21% /
fs-db4c8192.efs.us-east-1.amazonaws.com:/  8.0E  2.2T  8.0E   1% /opt

2.2T，一年前是3.9T。 请注意，仍远未达到 8 艾字节。

每天晚上整夜构建编译器

我们每天晚上都从头开始构建一堆编译器：GCC 主干、Clang 主干，以及用于反射、契约、协程和所有其他有趣东西的实验分支的长尾。 目前每晚新增就业岗位 94 个11，高于一年前的 73 个和 2022 年的 33 个。

它们在 EC2 上我们自己的 GitHub Actions 运行器上运行，通过优秀的 terraform-aws-github-runner 按需启动，所有编译器编排都是我们的。 构建主干 LLVM 需要一台大型机器和相当多的时间，而当我们设置它时，GitHub 的托管运行程序无法胜任。

每当有人要求我们提供另一个编译器并且我们答应时，这就是账单的一部分。

那些半成品的碎片

我们已经构建但尚未完成推出的一件事是我们所说的 CE 路由器：一个小型队列，其工作是决定应该在哪里进行编译，在 DynamoDB 中查找答案并将请求放到 SQS 队列上，结果通过 API 网关 WebSocket 返回到您的浏览器。 关键是要停止应答 HTTP 请求的机器，该机器必须是拥有编译器的机器。

它可以工作，但它还没有承载生产流量：通过它发送编译的负载均衡器规则仍然被注释掉，我们正在逐步迁移。 您今天的编译仍然像往常一样直接进入产品队列中的机器。

不过，构建它确实给 AWS 带来了一个很好的陷阱。 API Gateway WebSocket 帧的最大大小为 32KiB，几乎任何重要程序的程序集都比这个大；另一方面，SQS 消息的上限为 256KB，一个相当大小的多文件项目将超过这个上限。 因此，在两个方向上，如果东西太大，我们会将其推入 S3 并发送密钥。

其他一切

分散的其他服务各自完成一项工作：

  • DynamoDB 保存短链接。 每个 godbolt.org/z/... 你放入的幻灯片是表格中的一排，并且有几百万个。
  • S3 保存着我们构建的编译器、静态资产、日志和每日过期的内容可寻址编译缓存，因此第二个编译相同内容的人可以免费获得它。
  • Lambda 做一些奇怪的工作：Claude Expand 后端、夜间版本跟踪，以及将 CloudWatch 警报推送到我们的 Discord 中，这样不仅仅是我的手机在凌晨 3 点嗡嗡作响。
  • Route 53、ACM、CloudTrail、Backup 和 SES 是管道。 我不太想他们。
  • CloudWatch 驱动自动缩放触发器，但为了实际查看我们运行 Grafana、Prometheus 和 Loki 的东西。 这些仪表板是公开的。

一切都在 us-east-1 中。 如果您在悉尼进行编译，您的代码会走很长一段路，而且我担心它会继续这样做：保持几 TB 的编译器跨区域同步绝对是一场噩梦。

一些数字

我们将每个编译的高度匿名 JSON 记录记录到 S3 中，顶部有一个 Glue 表，因此在编写本文时，我正确地计算了它们：7 月份有 5,238,210 个编译，过去 12 个月有 7870 万个编译。 全年气温一直在缓慢下滑，比去年秋天的峰值下降了约三分之一。

去年每月的编译量。 从该脚本生成。

在此之前的大幅下降，从 2024 年的每月 1400 万，我至少可以解释一半：在 2024 年中期，我们将自动重新编译之前的默认延迟增加了一倍，从 750 毫秒到 1500 毫秒，然后到 2 秒13。 如果你连续打字，延迟加倍大约会使你生成的编译数量减半，而没有人注意到任何事情。 不过，这张最新的幻灯片并非如此：它是在一年多之后开始的。

所以我真的没有一个很好的解释，我也不能轻易地找到一个，因为我们故意不跟踪你是谁：没有cookies，没有任何东西可以让我告诉你昨天有多少人使用了该网站。 我每次都会再次进行这种交易，但这确实让我偶尔会眯着眼睛看图表。

自从我打开查询以来，以下是人们在 7 月份实际编译的内容：

最上面的条目占所有内容的 26%——大致相当于您默认的情况15。 负载均衡器每月收到约 1400 万个请求；今年我们最繁忙的一天是 4 月 21 日，有 144 万。 自动缩放本身就解决了这个问题；我是在写这篇文章的时候才知道的。

目前，我们在 AWS 上的所有这些费用每月约为 3,600 美元，每个编译的费用约为 0.0007 美元14。 在一年的大部分时间里，我们几乎没有支付任何费用：AWS 的开源积分几乎涵盖了所有费用。 这些在春天就用完了，我们自己支付了几个月的费用，AWS 刚刚将它们续订了一年，这是一个巨大的帮助。 无论哪种方式，我们都可以赚钱，这要感谢我们的 Patreon 支持者、GitHub 赞助商和商业赞助商。 我去年对成本进行了全面的细分，结果仍然大致正确。

编译器之墙，一年过去了：涵盖 93 种语言的 6,157 个条目。从与去年相同的脚本重新生成。

我仍然想解决的问题

部署比以前更好了，但其中的指导性工作仍然比我想象的要多16。 CE 路由器迁移已经“接近完成”有一段时间了…… 我仍然希望一开始就正确地布局 NFS 目录结构，而不是在长达十年的时间里一次只开发一个编译器。 今年我们将所有内容都迁移到了 Ubuntu 24.04，这并不是听起来那么整洁的小升级17。

这些都不是特别聪明：它是一个负载均衡器、一些充满廉价现货实例的扩展组、一个网络文件系统和十年来积累的黑客攻击。 不过，它确实可以继续工作，而且现在它基本上可以继续工作，而无需任何人去戳它。 我对此很满意。
